object_types.name: Account
object_types.definition: A customer account that holds subscriptions and is identified by a unique account number. Represents the billing entity in the system.

source_references.excerpt: Every account has an account number. That's what everything hangs off... Six digits, sequential, never reused.

object_types.name: AccountNumber
object_types.definition: A six-digit unique identifier for an account, assigned sequentially and never reused even if the account closes.

source_references.excerpt: Every account has an account number... Six digits, sequential, never reused.

object_types.name: Subscription
object_types.definition: An agreement between an account and the company specifying a product, price plan, and billing cycle. Identified by a subscription ID.

source_references.excerpt: A subscription is the agreement that this account pays us this amount on this cycle for this thing. It's got a subscription ID... Unique. Generated, prefixed with SUB.

object_types.name: SubscriptionId
object_types.definition: A unique identifier for a subscription, generated and prefixed with SUB.

source_references.excerpt: It's got a subscription ID... Unique. Generated, prefixed with SUB.

object_types.name: Product
object_types.definition: A product offering that customers can subscribe to. Currently three products exist: CORE, ANALYTICS, and CONNECT.

source_references.excerpt: Product code. We have three: CORE, ANALYTICS, and CONNECT... Fixed today.

object_types.name: ProductCode
object_types.definition: A code identifying a product. Fixed set of three: CORE, ANALYTICS, CONNECT.

source_references.excerpt: Product code. We have three: CORE, ANALYTICS, and CONNECT... Fixed today.

object_types.name: PricePlan
object_types.definition: A billing artifact that specifies the price and billing frequency for a feature bundle. Identified by a plan code (e.g., CORE-MO-49, CORE-AN-490). Multiple price plans can map to the same feature bundle.

source_references.excerpt: The price plan. It's got a plan code, it says what the customer pays and how often. CORE-MO-49, CORE-AN-490, that kind of thing.

object_types.name: PlanCode
object_types.definition: A unique code identifying a price plan, such as CORE-MO-49 or CORE-AN-490.

source_references.excerpt: It's got a plan code... CORE-MO-49, CORE-AN-490, that kind of thing.

object_types.name: FeatureBundle
object_types.definition: A feature offering that defines what customers get, identified by name. Examples: Starter, Professional, Enterprise. Each price plan entitles exactly one feature bundle.

source_references.excerpt: When I say plan I mean what the customer gets. Starter, Professional, Enterprise. It's the feature bundle -- how many seats, whether they get the API, whether they get SSO.
Name. Starter, Professional, Enterprise. There's no code, which annoys me... Is the name unique? Yes. There's exactly one Professional.

object_types.name: BundleName
object_types.definition: A unique name identifying a feature bundle, such as Starter, Professional, or Enterprise.

source_references.excerpt: Name... Is the name unique? Yes. There's exactly one Professional.

object_types.name: SubscriptionStartDate
object_types.definition: The date on which a subscription begins. Mandatory for every subscription.

source_references.excerpt: Start date is always there. You can't create a subscription without one, the form won't submit.

object_types.name: SubscriptionEndDate
object_types.definition: The date on which a subscription terminates. Optional; open-ended subscriptions have no end date.

source_references.excerpt: An open-ended subscription has no end date. Most of them are open-ended -- they run until cancelled. A fixed-term one has an end date agreed up front.

object_types.name: BillingPeriod
object_types.definition: The frequency of billing for a subscription: monthly or annual. Every subscription has exactly one, never both and never neither.

source_references.excerpt: Billing period -- what are the values? Monthly or annual... You cannot bill someone monthly and annually for the same subscription, that's just billing them twice.
Every subscription has exactly one billing period.

object_types.name: SubscriptionStatus
object_types.definition: The operational status of a subscription. Exactly one of: trialing, active, past due, or cancelled. Note: 'paused' exists as a separate boolean flag but is not a formal status.

source_references.excerpt: Status? Trialing, active, past due, cancelled... Exactly one, yes.

object_types.name: PlanChange
object_types.definition: A record of a plan change on a subscription, capturing the new price plan, effective date, and requester. Identified by a change ID. Maintains the history of plan modifications.

source_references.excerpt: A change is a record... It's got a change ID... It has to, because we need to know who made it and when it takes effect, and those are different dates... It records the subscription, the new price plan, the effective date, and who requested it.

object_types.name: ChangeId
object_types.definition: A unique identifier for a plan change record.

source_references.excerpt: It's got a change ID.

object_types.name: EffectiveDate
object_types.definition: The date on which a plan change takes effect. Can differ from the date the change was requested.

source_references.excerpt: Someone can make a change on the third that takes effect on the first of next month.

object_types.name: Requester
object_types.definition: The person or system that requested a plan change.

ambiguities.description: Plan ambiguity: Three different concepts are all called 'plan' in the system. (1) Price Plan: the billing artifact (plan code) that specifies price and billing frequency. (2) Feature Bundle: the feature offering ('Starter', 'Professional', 'Enterprise') that defines what customers get. (3) Sales/Negotiated Plan: a custom deal negotiated by the sales team, which may match neither of the above. The transcript acknowledges this ambiguity but does not resolve it. The model captures Price Plan and Feature Bundle as separate entities, but the Sales Plan is not formally modeled. This could lead to confusion when stakeholders use the term 'plan' without qualification.

source_references.excerpt: Tom: The price plan... CORE-MO-49, CORE-AN-490, that kind of thing. Priya: And I mean the billing artefact... Tom: When I say plan I mean what the customer gets. Starter, Professional, Enterprise... and the sales team calls a third thing a plan, which is the deal they negotiated
we still call three different things 'plan' and this document won't fix that. It won't. But it'll at least name them separately, which is a start.

ambiguities.description: Paused status: The system has a 'paused' flag that behaves like a status but is not formally part of the four-status enum (trialing, active, past due, cancelled). It exists as a separate boolean and can overlap confusingly with the active status -- querying for active subscriptions may return paused ones. The relationship between the paused flag and the four formal statuses is unclear. Should paused be a fifth status, or remain separate? This could affect reporting and business logic.

source_references.excerpt: Tom: There's also paused. Priya: Paused isn't a status, it's a flag... If you ask the system for active subscriptions you get paused ones too.
I'm going to record the four statuses as the status, and note that paused exists separately and overlaps confusingly.

ambiguities.description: Mid-term annual subscription cancellation refund policy: When an annual subscription is cancelled mid-term, the system sets the end date to the paid-through date and access continues. There is no refund mechanism in the subscription system. However, manual credits have been issued four times in the past quarter as 'goodwill'. It is unclear whether this is an undocumented policy or case-by-case exceptions. From a revenue perspective (Sam's concern), it is not clear whether these should be treated as contra-revenue or refund liability. The business rule for mid-term cancellation refunds is unresolved and deferred to finance and legal.

source_references.excerpt: Someone signs an annual deal in January, pays up front, cancels in April. What happens? ...They've paid for the year, they keep access until December, we don't refund... cancellation on an annual subscription sets the end date to the paid-through date and access continues.

Four times in a quarter isn't goodwill, it's a policy nobody's written down... From a revenue perspective I need to know whether to treat those as contra-revenue or as a refund liability, and right now I decide case by case... the system rule is clear, and what's unclear is whether the system rule is the business rule.
cancellation sets an end date and access runs to it, and it will not invent a refund concept that doesn't exist... Put my name on wanting that resolved.

ambiguities.description: Current plan derivation vs. denormalization: Sam initially stated that MRR is 'worked out' and derived from price plan and billing period, and questioned whether a subscription has a current plan field. Priya clarified that the subscription DOES carry a denormalised current_plan field (maintained by the change process) alongside the change history. Sam withdrew his correction. However, the exact mechanism for maintaining consistency between the denormalised current plan and the change history is unclear. What happens if they disagree? Priya states 'if those two ever disagree, the change history wins and the current plan is the bug' -- implying the change history is the system of record. This suggests the current plan is a computed cache, not a true independent fact, but it is stored. The model should clarify whether current plan is stored for performance or is authoritative.

source_references.excerpt: Every subscription has an MRR... It's on the subscription in the reporting layer... It's worked out. It's the plan price normalised to a month... Nobody types an MRR anywhere.

You said a subscription belongs to one price plan. It doesn't, really -- that's what the plan changes are for... No, Sam, it does have a current plan field... Since the reporting rebuild. It's maintained by the change process, nobody sets it by hand... if those two ever disagree, the change history wins and the current plan is the bug.

ambiguities.description: MRR as derived vs. reportable: Sam initially referred to MRR as 'a field on the subscription in the reporting layer' and later caught himself, clarifying that it is 'worked out' (computed) and 'nothing writes it'. However, Sam still sees it in his dashboards. The model treats MRR as a derived calculation and does not store it as a fact. However, if MRR is computed differently in reporting than in the source system, or if there are edge cases (e.g., zero-price plans, promotional offers), the derivation rule may be incomplete. The exact formula for computing MRR and the scope of its application (all subscriptions, only active, etc.) should be confirmed.

source_references.excerpt: Every subscription has an MRR... It's on the subscription in the reporting layer... It's worked out. It's the plan price normalised to a month. An annual plan at 490 is an MRR of 40.83... Nobody types an MRR anywhere... I called it a field because that's how I see it in my dashboards, but nothing writes it.
I'm not going to model it as an attribute of the subscription, then, because it isn't a fact anybody asserts -- it's a calculation over facts we already have... It'd be wrong within a month.

ambiguities.description: Halloway Group incident constraint enforcement: The constraint 'one active subscription per account per product' was implemented in response to the Halloway Group incident, where the same account had two subscriptions to the same product under different team members and was billed twice for eight months. The constraint is now enforced at the database level. However, the model assumes this constraint applies to all accounts and all time. The possibility of historical data (pre-constraint) containing violations, or the need to track the period of enforcement, is not discussed. Should the model include a temporal aspect (constraint effective date) or assume the constraint has always applied?

source_references.excerpt: An account has one active subscription per account per product... One active subscription per account per product, enforced at the database level.
We billed them twice for eight months... one active subscription per account per product, enforced at the database level. Yes.

ambiguities.description: Billing period as exclusive constraint: The model states that a subscription has exactly one billing period (monthly or annual) and cannot be both. However, there is a narrative comment that 'there was a quarterly once, for one customer, and it caused so much trouble that we bought them out of it.' This implies quarterly was once a valid value. The model treats monthly and annual as fixed, but it is unclear whether the value set could expand in the future (as Tom mentions 'a fourth product in discovery'). Should the value constraint on BillingPeriod be extensible, or is it truly fixed?

source_references.excerpt: Billing period -- what are the values? Monthly or annual... There was a quarterly once, for one customer, and it caused so much trouble that we bought them out of it.

ambiguities.description: Product set stability: The model records three products (CORE, ANALYTICS, CONNECT) as of the current date. Tom states 'Fixed today' and mentions 'a fourth in discovery, but I'm not going to pretend I know what it is.' The model does not assume the fourth product exists in the data, but it is unclear how to handle future product additions. Should the value constraint on ProductCode be versioned, or are we modeling the system as it exists today only?

source_references.excerpt: We have three: CORE, ANALYTICS, and CONNECT... Fixed today. There's a fourth in discovery, but I'm not going to pretend I know what it is.

ambiguities.description: Feature bundle lifecycle before pricing: Tom states that a feature bundle can exist without a price plan ('we build a bundle before we price it. Enterprise existed for two months before there was anything to buy'). This means a FeatureBundle can exist with zero price plans pointing at it. The model captures this as optional participation on the FeatureBundle side of the 'PricePlan entitles FeatureBundle' relationship. However, the commercial or operational implications (e.g., can a subscription reference a non-priced bundle?) are not discussed.

source_references.excerpt: Can a bundle exist with no price plan pointing at it? Yes -- we build a bundle before we price it. Enterprise existed for two months before there was anything to buy.

ambiguities.description: Multiple price plans per bundle and legacy plans: The model captures that many price plans can entitle the same feature bundle. Priya mentions 'bespoke enterprise pricing' plans for individual customers, and Tom mentions 'legacy' plans that have not been retired. It is unclear how to distinguish bespoke/custom price plans from standard ones, or when a legacy plan should be retired. Should the model track plan status (active, legacy, draft) or a creation/retirement date?

source_references.excerpt: There's a monthly and an annual for each bundle, and sometimes a legacy one we haven't retired... And there are price plans that exist only for one customer. Bespoke enterprise pricing.

ambiguities.description: Plan change history completeness: A new subscription starts with no plan changes (line 221-223). However, the model does not capture when a subscription is initially created. Is the initial plan assignment a 'plan change' or a separate create operation? If it is not recorded as a change, then the initial plan (and effective date) is only available on the subscription itself. If a new plan change overwrites the current_plan field, how do you recover the original plan? The history model should clarify whether the subscription's initial state is recorded as a change or separately.

source_references.excerpt: Can a subscription have many changes? Over its life, yes, plenty... A brand new subscription has none.

ambiguities.description: Plan change request date vs. effective date: The model captures that a plan change has an effective date distinct from the request date ('Someone can make a change on the third that takes effect on the first of next month'). However, the request date is not explicitly captured in the model. It is attributed to the Requester field, but Requester is defined as 'the person or system that requested' not 'the date of the request'. Should the model include a separate 'RequestDate' or 'CreatedDate' fact type on PlanChange?

source_references.excerpt: Someone can make a change on the third that takes effect on the first of next month.
